Issued at 613 PM EDT Tue Oct 13 2026

The long term forecast period is defined by a significant change in 
sensible weather conditions across Eastern Kentucky. While the 
period begins on an unseasonably warm and wet note on Thursday, a 
potent cold front should sweep through the area on Friday and usher 
in a noticeably cooler and drier airmass for the weekend. In fact, 
Saturday's forecast features the coldest temperatures of the season 
thus far. A widespread frost is looking increasingly likely on 
Saturday night, but temperatures are forecast to moderate back 
towards climatological norms under fair skies early next week. 

When the period opens on Thursday morning, the boundary responsible 
for Wednesday's convection will likely be stalled out in the 
vicinity of the Ohio River Valley. Its parent shortwave disturbance 
will have propagated off to the NE aloft, leaving zonal flow in 
place over the forecast area. So, in the absence of meaningful 
advection, rain chances remain in the forecast on Thursday. The 
highest PoPs are resolved closer to the stalled boundary in the 
northern half of the forecast area, but this does not align with the 
warmest temperatures. Persistent sky cover should limit highs to the 
upper 70s/near 80 in the places that are most likely to experience 
additional rain showers. While those forecast highs are still above 
average for this time of year, they are 5+ degrees cooler than they 
were on Wednesday. This corresponds with a lower risk for heavy 
rainfall and stronger storms, and the risk for hazardous weather 
appears low on Thursday. 

The attention subsequently turns upstream towards the Great Plains, 
where the next impactful storm system will be setting up. A sharp 
trough ejecting southeast out of Canada will phase with a leeward 
Rocky Mountain trough to yield a deeper, positively-tilted feature 
over the Upper Midwest on Thursday evening. Vertically-stacked 
southwesterly flow around the base of that trough will advect warm 
air into the atmospheric column over the Ohio River Valley. The 
aforementioned boundary is accordingly forecast to lift back north 
as a warm front on Thursday night, and a deepening surface low 
should emerge over the Great Lakes by Friday morning. In response to 
the tightening pressure gradient, winds will become breezy 
overnight. This will prevent the area's conventional ridge-valley 
splits from materializing in this time frame, as the boundary layer 
should remain well mixed. Given the lack of decoupling and the warm 
air advection regime in place, Thursday night's temperature forecast 
looks unseasonably mild. Expect a muted diurnal heating curve, with 
lows in the mid to upper 60s. 

Friday's high temperatures will be pretty similar to Thursday 
night's lows, as the cold front associated with this system will be 
on the doorstep of the JKL CWA on Friday morning. There should be 
enough forced lift for some generic rain showers over the CWA during 
and after Friday's frontal passage, but the greatest impacts from 
this boundary will stem from its cold air advection. The sharp 
nature of the parent troughing aloft and the fairly tight surface 
pressure gradient in this set up collectively suggest that there 
will be a pronounced shift from breezy southwesterly winds to 
gustier northwesterly winds as frontal passage occurs on Friday. 
Northwesterly wind gusts in the 20-30 mph range are likely on Friday 
afternoon/evening before the pressure gradient weakens overnight. 
The winds will retain their northwesterly orientation through 
Saturday morning, which will help them usher a noticeably cooler and 
drier airmass into the region for the weekend. That efficient cold 
air advection may actually cause temperatures to decrease during the 
afternoon hours on Friday, with widespread temps in the 50s by 
Friday evening and the 40s on Saturday morning.

Northerly winds associated with a post-frontal surface high will 
keep the cold air advection going on Saturday. High temps will 
struggle to make it out of the 50s, and afternoon dewpoints should 
plummet towards the low/mid 30s area-wide. Under mostly clear skies 
and slackening winds, Saturday night looks to be the coldest night 
of the season thus far. Efficient radiational cooling and those dry 
dewpoint values favor widespread low temperatures in the 30s and 
frost potential in more than just the typical cold spots. Near-
freezing temperatures cannot be ruled out in the most sheltered and 
shadiest valley locales, but a widespread freeze appears unlikely. 
Nevertheless, frost/freeze headline products will need to be 
considered as this time frame approaches and forecast confidence 
continues to improve. Agricultural interests and recreational 
gardeners are accordingly encouraged to review any relevant frost 
preparedness plans and stay tuned for potential product issuance.
